articles.title: Russell Brand accuser says alleged rape left her afraid she may be pregnant
articles.summary: The 51-year-old faces three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.
articles.body:
Warning - this report contains graphic content

A woman who alleges Russell Brand raped her in a hotel room has said he turned from "camp, friendly and effeminate" to "monster-like" before the alleged assault.

The 51-year-old actor and comedian faces seven charges - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.

The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies the charges.

One of the women told the jury at Southwark Crown Court on Thursday: "He was just dark and arrogant and performing - he was scary, he was demanding."

The woman told police she met Brand before he was famous while attending the Labour Party conference in Bournemouth in 1999. She alleges he later raped her.

The woman said she was left feeling "dirty" and afraid she may be pregnant in the aftermath of the alleged attack.

Before the alleged rape, the woman also said Brand made her take photos of him with his top off, which were shown to the jury.

The jury were played a police interview with the woman recorded in 2023, when reporting the alleged crime, before she was called to the witness box on Thursday.

The complainant said she and Brand had gone back to a hotel room. She told the police officer she thought Brand "was gay" when they met earlier and she didn't feel like he was "trying it on with her".

The woman said she had been in the bathroom, but when she came out "he had like briefs on - and I was like taken aback and shocked. He was prancing around".

The complainant alleged Brand told her: "Don't worry, that's how I am."

She recalled thinking "what on earth have I got into" when, she claims, a shirtless Brand made her take photos of him before the alleged attack.

She was heard telling the officer: "I'm reporting that Russell Brand did rape me.

"What I'm going to say now - then, I second guessed myself if it was rape because it was so normal.

"Sorry... he raped me basically - I know that happened. I remember him touching my breasts a lot - while kissing my neck."

During the video evidence, Brand watched the TV screen attached to the dock - rarely taking his eyes away. He appeared to be listening attentively and hardly moved his position throughout.

Describing the alleged encounter, the woman later told the jury: "He was big, I felt threatened and he's half-naked... I didn't think at that point his intentions were good."

"He was the centre of the show, it was like it was back on stage – he wasn't the [same] person I was chatting to."

She added: "He just changed suddenly from this... camp, friendly and effeminate to monster-like."

The woman recounted to police how Brand acted "like Basil Fawlty when he does his goose steps" before the alleged rape.

She told the officer: "I remember him being like an ostrich - like a bird because he was very leggy.

"I wasn't laughing, I just remember him jumping up and down being silly."

The woman said after Brand left the room she was "just sitting there crying and I felt stupid," adding: "In that moment in time I was just shocked."

At one point in the police interview, she cried while saying "this was something dirty that had happened".

She said she "thought it was my fault", adding that she was "having nightmares" about the possibility of being pregnant.

The complainant said she had delayed coming forward because she was worried it would impact her professional life. "I was told if you come out with this, your career is done," she said.

Under cross-examination Brand's barrister, Ian Winter KC put it to the complainant that when she first met Brand she welcomed his attention.

"I welcomed his company, not what followed," the woman replied.

He then suggested that she fell under his spell and that she wanted to spend more time with him.

The woman replied: "That's incorrect. I did not fall under his spell and I did not find him attractive. "

Asked by the defence why she agreed to go back to the hotel room with Brand, she responded: "I'm telling you... I thought he was a gay man, very softly spoken, very effeminate.

"I felt safe – I felt sexually safe with him. He was very intelligent and that appealed to me, not in a sexual sense. "

The woman became tearful a number of times while giving her evidence from the witness box.

At one point the judge told the witness to "take a moment, catch your breath", after she became emotional.

Brand's barrister later challenged the complainant about why she did not run back into the bathroom or leave the room when she realised Brand had removed some of his clothes.

She replied: "What was I supposed to do? Hide in bathroom? Walk out the room? Walk past him? I had no phone, no reception, no idea where I was. Run into the night with him following me?"

Referring to photographs she had taken of Brand, she said: "I took those photographs, he told me to take them, he was showing off, he was prancing around... I was scared... I couldn't fight him.

"I blame myself for allowing him back into my room," the woman said.

She was also challenged by the defence barrister about why she didn't report her allegation about Brand to the police in Bournemouth.

She said: "I didn't report it as I didn't want anyone to know. I didn't think anyone would believe me."

The woman told the jury that after she says she was raped by Brand she blamed herself "in that moment".

"I hate that I blamed myself, I shouldn't have to blame myself."

She also told jurors: "I regret to this day the error in judgment thinking this man would not rape me.

Russell Brand denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.

He has said that any sexual contact if it happened, would have been consensual.

The trial continues and is expected to last for six weeks.

Brand rose to fame as a stand-up comedian and became a household name as host of TV shows such as Big Brother's Big Mouth, and with his own radio programmes on stations including BBC Radio 2 and 6 Music.

He went on to establish a Hollywood career, starring in films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him To The Greek. In recent years, he has turned to podcasting and now lives in Florida in the United States.

articles.title: Investigators zero in on possible cause of Wisconsin plane crash that killed 6
articles.summary: Flight data shows the Piper Malibu's airspeed nearly doubled to 340 mph as it plunged at 4,000 feet per minute after the pilot reported wing icing.
articles.body: A small plane that crashed in Wisconsin, killing six people, including a child, had plummeted toward the ground at a rate of up to 4,000 feet per minute after its pilot reported ice accumulating on the wings, according to newly released flight data and federal investigators. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said the pilot of the Piper PA-46 Malibu was flying at 24,000 feet on Tuesday night when he alerted air traffic control to ice building up on the aircraft's wings and requested permission to descend. Air traffic controllers approved the request, but the plane entered a descending right turn that became increasingly sharp before communications and flight tracking data were lost, investigators said. COAST GUARD SUSPENDS SEARCH FOR BOSTON-BOUND MEDEVAC PLANE OFF NANTUCKET WITH 6 ON BOARD Data from FlightRadar24 showed the plane's airspeed nearly doubled to 340 mph as it descended at a rate of up to 4,000 feet per minute, according to The Associated Press. "It has all the earmarks of an icing-related loss of control," aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti, a former investigator for both the NTSB and Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), told the outlet. Ice accumulation poses a serious threat to aircraft because even a thin layer can disrupt airflow over the wings, reducing lift and making a plane more difficult to control. The six-seat, single-engine aircraft was traveling from Kenosha to Menomonie when it crashed shortly before 10 p.m. in a wooded area of Sauk County near Mirror Lake State Park, about 10 miles west of Wisconsin Dells, authorities said. Rain was falling as a thunderstorm moved through Dellona at the time of the crash. FATAL AIR AMBULANCE CRASH EXPOSES GROWING GPS DANGER FACING US FLIGHTS All six people aboard were killed. Authorities said no structures were damaged and no one on the ground was injured. The identities of the victims had not been publicly released. The Piper Malibu model has previously faced federal scrutiny over crashes involving icing conditions. The NTSB conducted a special safety review of seven icing-related crashes involving Piper Malibu and Mirage aircraft between 1989 and 1991, several of which involved relatively inexperienced pilots unfamiliar with handling the sophisticated planes in icy conditions. The review prompted recommendations for changes to pilot training, aircraft checklists and operating manuals, as well as the addition of an indicator light for systems designed to prevent ice buildup in pitot tubes, which help provide accurate airspeed readings. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The NTSB is leading the investigation into Tuesday's crash. Investigators have not determined an official cause. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Philadelphia artist Isaiah Zagar turned bottles, bike wheels and ceramic shards into a 3,000-square-foot maze; after a 2004 threat to dismantle it, the community saved it and tickets now frequently sell out
articles.summary: Discover the breathtaking Philadelphia's Magic Gardens, a 3,000-square-foot mosaic maze created by artist Isaiah Zagar. Learn how a community came together to save this unique art installation and what visitors can experience today in this vibrant cultural landmark.
articles.body: A vacant plot in Philadelphia became the canvas for artist Isaiah Zagar, who spent years transforming discarded bottles, bicycle wheels, ceramic fragments and mirrors into an intricate maze of mosaics. Spread across more than 3,000 square feet, Philadelphia’s Magic Gardens survived a threat of demolition in 2004 after residents and art supporters joined forces to preserve it.The site has since developed into a museum featuring winding passages, tunnels, indoor galleries and a two-level outdoor sculpture garden.Zagar, who died in February 2026, left behind a public artwork shaped by his life, travels and interest in folk art. His creation also reflects how a community can help protect an artistic space that might otherwise have disappeared.How did Isaiah Zagar create Philadelphia’s Magic Gardens?Born in Philadelphia in 1939 and raised in Brooklyn, Zagar studied painting and graphics at the Pratt Institute of Art in New York, according to the Magic Gardens website. His interest in large-scale art environments began when he was 19 and encountered the work of artist Clarence Schmidt in Woodstock, New York.Zagar and his wife, Julia Zagar, met in 1963 and married three months later. They later joined the Peace Corps as conscientious objectors to the Vietnam War and worked with local folk artists in Peru. Their time there deepened their interest in handmade art, cultural traditions and community collaboration.After returning to the United States in 1967, Zagar taught himself to create mosaics while recovering from a mental health crisis. Julia opened the Eye’s Gallery on Philadelphia’s South Street, where the couple lived above the shop. Zagar began decorating the building, marking the start of a long period of transforming walls and buildings into art environments.In 1986 and 1995, the couple bought two buildings and a lot to serve as Zagar’s studio. After completing mosaics across those spaces, he began working on neighbouring vacant lots that he did not own. He decorated the fences and gradually built structures using found objects.The resulting installation combined everyday materials with handmade tiles, mirrors, bicycle spokes, bottles and objects collected from different places. Zagar used these pieces to reflect his personal experiences and artistic influences.Why was the artwork nearly dismantled in 2004?The future of the installation became uncertain in 2004, when the Boston-based owner of the land discovered the work and decided to sell the property. The owner called for the installation to be dismantled.The prospect of losing the artwork prompted neighbours, lawyers and art supporters to step in. Their efforts helped establish the nonprofit organisation Philadelphia’s Magic Gardens, which purchased the grounds and took responsibility for preserving the site.The campaign turned a privately created art environment into a community-supported cultural attraction. Following the organisation’s formation, Zagar continued expanding the installation, excavating tunnels and grottos and covering additional surfaces with mosaics.The main structures were completed by 2008, although Zagar continued adding elements with the organisation’s preservation team during his lifetime.What can visitors see at Philadelphia’s Magic Gardens?The attraction covers indoor and outdoor areas equivalent to roughly half a city block. Its two indoor galleries host changing exhibitions by artists from Philadelphia and elsewhere, while the outdoor garden features winding tiled passages, sculptures and mosaics arranged across two levels.The installation is built from an unusual mix of materials, including cement, ceramic shards, bottles, bicycle wheels and mirrors. These objects form patterns and structures that visitors can explore on foot, with sections running both above and below ground.The museum also organises guided tours, family activities, art workshops and evening events featuring live music. Its programmes extend beyond Zagar’s work by showcasing other artists and offering visitors opportunities to learn about mosaic-making and creative reuse.Philadelphia’s Magic Gardens now operates as an independent nonprofit.Zagar donated the Magic Gardens StudioZagar created art environments across Philadelphia and beyond, producing mosaics on more than 200 public walls over a career spanning more than five decades. His work is held in collections including the Philadelphia Museum of Art and the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts.In 2023, Isaiah and Julia donated the Magic Gardens Studio, along with artworks stored there, to the nonprofit organisation. The move was intended to help protect their work for future generations.Zagar died in February 2026 from complications arising from heart failure and Parkinson’s disease. Julia continues to live near the museum and runs the Eye’s Gallery.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: El-Sayed's own words reveal a radical plan to dismantle the Second Amendment
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed floated replacing the Second Amendment in a video he later made private, raising alarms about his gun control agenda in Michigan.
articles.body: "What if we tweaked the Constitution, amended the Second Amendment, and instead of the right to bear arms, we change it to the right to have healthcare?" That is not a college activist. That is Abdul El-Sayed — the Democratic nominee for United States Senate in Michigan — talking into his own camera, on his own channel. And it is one of many videos that he quietly made private from his channel once he decided he wanted a seat in the world’s most powerful legislative body. A U.S. Senate nominee from one of the two major national parties, who has a legitimate chance to win, actively floated the idea of replacing the Second Amendment — not merely regulating it, which would be bad enough. This is not your typical anti-gun Democrat rhetoric. This is a dangerous and new precedent coming from far-left Democrats. They realize the courts are increasingly unwilling to permit them to regulate our right to keep and bear arms. Just recently, in ANJRPC v. Attorney General of New Jersey, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit ruled that New Jersey’s ban on "assault weapons" and "high-capacity magazines" was unconstitutional. And in June, the U.S. Supreme Court agreed to hear a challenge to Cook County, Illinois’ ban on "assault weapons" and Connecticut’s ban on "high-capacity magazines" under Viramontes. INSIDE TRUMP'S UNPRECEDENTED BATTLE PLAN TO EXPAND SECOND AMENDMENT RIGHTS THROUGH JUSTICE DEPARTMENT However, Michiganders see through this charade. The infamous gun control group Moms Demand Action has endorsed El-Sayed. Moms Demand Action is the grassroots arm of Everytown for Gun Safety, an anti-gun organization whose one of its stated goals is to ban the most popular semi-automatic sporting rifle in America. And Michiganders know that El-Sayed is in favor of most, if not all, the policy objectives stated by Everytown for Gun Safety. In his 2018 run for governor of Michigan, El-Sayed supported an "assault weapons" ban, backed red flag laws and embraced a host of other anti-gun positions. The video in question is not the story — the video is the confession that explains the agenda. El-Sayed’s campaign responded to a CNN article about the deleted videos by saying, "Cherry-picked comments from old podcasts don’t reflect his beliefs today." But he never wanted nor expected these comments to surface — that’s why he tried to hide the video. When recently pressed by Jesse Watters at Fox on his comments to abolish the Second Amendment, El-Sayed dodged the question by claiming "people are more worried about whether or not they can see a doctor than whether or not they can have a gun." It would seem that CNN in fact did not cherry-pick comments. Time and time again, El-Sayed continues to prove to his future constituents that he would rather spill socialist talking points and implement a socialist agenda by decimating the U.S. Constitution. His goal is to erase any kind of national pride, the rights of Americans and the culture that makes this country the greatest in the history of the world. Electing someone like this to the United States Senate is dangerous and reckless. EL-SAYED ARGUED AGAINST THE SECOND AMENDMENT IN UNEARTHED SOCIAL MEDIA VIDEOS Plus, his most recent endorsement proves that El-Sayed intends to undermine Michiganders' Second Amendment rights. Former Congresswoman Gabrielle Giffords — infamous for calling for "no more guns" — along with her gun control group, just endorsed El-Sayed. In fact, in Giffords’ announcement of El-Sayed’s endorsement, El-Sayed himself said, "it’s an honor to receive the endorsement of Giffords PAC." This is not the statement from a candidate who supposedly regrets calling for the abolition of the Second Amendment. Anti-gunners like El-Sayed are terrified that by June 2027, the Supreme Court is likely to strike down these "assault weapon" bans as unconstitutional. This is apparently forcing candidates like El-Sayed and even California Governor Gavin Newsom, who wish to enact gun control, into taking the unprecedented stance that the Second Amendment needs to be repealed or replaced. DOJ THREATENS TO SUE CALIFORNIA OVER 'GLOCK BAN,' ARGUING LAW VIOLATES SECOND AMENDMENT El-Sayed’s campaign accuses CNN of cherry-picking the coverage of this story. Remember, he did not delete the video in question. He only set it to private. Here is what makes this more than a slip from an old podcast. Repealing a constitutional amendment requires 2/3 of both chambers of Congress and 38 states. It’s not going to happen. However, a senator confirms judges who interpret the Constitution. Every federal judge, circuit nominee and Supreme Court justice for the next six years runs through the chamber El-Sayed wants to join. A man who believes the Second Amendment protects nothing but state militias, does not need to repeal a single word. He only needs to vote, repeatedly, for anti-gun judges. For 30 years, gun control groups told us they only wanted "common sense" restrictions on the Second Amendment. Now that the courts are enforcing the right to bear arms as written, we are suddenly hearing that the Second Amendment itself should go. They are losing the argument about the Constitution — and their answer is to change the Constitution. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP So Mr. El-Sayed: be transparent with the voters you’re asking to hire you. On camera, in your own words, tell Michigan that you oppose an "assault weapons" ban. Until then, the video you made private stands as your truth.

articles.title: Lula or Bolsonaro: Why Brazil's presidential election matters for Brics and India
articles.summary: When Brics leaders met in New Delhi last month, Brazil’s President Lula da Silva was conspicuously absent from the Bharat Mandapam.
articles.body: When Brics leaders met in New Delhi last month, Brazil’s President Lula da Silva was conspicuously absent from the Bharat Mandapam. He was campaigning for the crucial fourth term back home, so his foreign minister Mauro Vieira arrived in the capital for the "non-West" summit.That absence could now highlight the Brics' road ahead, at least for the time US President Donald Trump occupies the White House.Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability. This is what Brics stood for when India hosted it on September 12. However, the real B of Brics, which is Brazil, has the world's attention.On 25 October, Brazilians will choose between Lula and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of jailed ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, and the winner will decide how deeply one of the bloc’s founding members keeps investing in it.Flávio Bolsonaro leads the race into the runoff (second round of voting) after securing 47 per cent of the first-round vote, against Lula’s 45 per cent. Brazil mandates a second round of voting if no candidate secures a majority (more than 50 per cent) in the first round. Therefore, for a grouping already stretched by its own expansion, the result matters well beyond South America.A bloc pulled in three directionsBrics began with five members and grew to eleven after the 2024 expansion, with Indonesia the newest, joining in 2025. Brazil opposed the enlargement, particularly because of the one nation. Iran. It feared that adding the avowedly anti-West Islamic Republic would cost the group its cohesion. Like India, Brazil wants Brics to be reformist and not revolutionary, thereby limiting it to a body that argues for change inside the existing order rather than one that tries to replace it.Vieira, putting the Brazilian view plainly in the run-up to the 2026 summit, said that “a multipolar world that promises peace and prosperity must not be confused with a world of spheres of influence.” In other words, Brasília wants rules that bind the strong as well as the weak.Brazil had some success as the New Delhi declaration reaffirmed support for the United Nations system and the Paris climate agreement, going further than the G7, whose latest declarations did not mention the climate pact.However, these are words and not actions, and Russia, a Brics member, has ignored the UN Charter in recent years. Even so, agreeing to acknowledge the UN’s legitimacy was a better outcome than blocking any mention of it.Those gains on paper may not last, as Brazil’s place in the bloc will depend largely on its next president. The world’s two biggest powers have very different visions for what Brics should become. Both Washington and Beijing are seeking to tilt the balance in their favour.The United States, under Donald Trump, has made clear what it wants from Brazil. The Trump administration imposed heavy trade duties on Brazilian exports in July 2025, in retaliation for what it called a judicial “witch hunt” against former President Jair Bolsonaro, who Trump see as his "ally".It has sanctioned the Supreme Court justice who prosecuted him and revoked the visas of several justices. It also accepted Flávio Bolsonaro’s appeal in May to designate two Brazilian criminal groups as foreign terrorist organisations, while Lula’s alternative proposals went unanswered.Beyond one man’s fateA Bolsonaro win would help realign Latin America behind an America First agenda of militarised approaches to crime, crackdowns on migration and preferential access to critical minerals and energy. Brazil holds the world’s second-largest rare earth reserves, and Washington wants to reduce its dependence on China for them.On the trade and commerce front, Bolsonaro has criticised non-dollar initiatives, which is exactly the kind of de-dollarisation talk that makes some Brics ideas unwelcome in Washington. His platform does not mention Brics at all, and he has entertained the idea of leaving the group.Beijing sits on the other side of the ledger, and its leverage is economic. China has been Brazil’s largest trading partner since 2009. It buys nearly 30 per cent of Brazil’s total exports, including soybeans, crude oil and iron ore, and it has become a major investor in electricity, mining, cars and oil.A Brics that China hopes to make firmer and more assertive is difficult to build without Brazil, the largest economy in Latin America. That is why a Brazilian drift towards Washington would be felt in Beijing, even if it never became a formal exit.Nevertheless, the challenge with China is intricate, as even under Jair Bolsonaro, anti-Beijing rhetoric did not stop bilateral trade from reaching record levels, and Brazil resisted US pressure to exclude Huawei from its 5G rollout. Flávio Bolsonaro’s own programme envisages continued commercial engagement with China. A withdrawal from Brics, in short, is possible but far from inevitable.Therefore, a Bolsonaro government could stay inside the main multilateral bodies while withdrawing from the effort to give them energy, shifting from coalition-building among middle powers to a transactional, bilateral relationship with Washington.Lula, by contrast, has pursued what officials call “multi-alignment”, keeping a working relationship with the United States, expanding trade with China and using Brics, the G20 and UN climate talks to widen Brazil’s room for manoeuvre.A state under strainThe foreign policy debate is real, but it is not what most Brazilians say drives their vote. Crime is a central worry, and Bolsonaro’s “mano dura”, or iron fist, approach appeals to voters tired of violence in their neighbourhoods.Education is another concern, as a recent poll found that 71 per cent of Brazilians are weighing it in their vote, and 83 per cent believe it should be among the next government’s top three priorities.Only 66 per cent of Grade 2 children met basic literacy requirements in 2025, well short of the 80 per cent target for 2030.On the US relationship, voters appear to lean towards Lula. Polls show his popularity rose after his frequent disagreements with Trump over trade and security, and other surveys found Brazilians blamed Bolsonaro more for the tariffs imposed in July.The Brazilian Association of Institutional and Governmental Relations says the same pressure would follow Bolsonaro into office.Its president, Jean Castro, said: “He cannot adopt a stance that could be mistaken for subservience.”Behind these campaign themes lies a harder question. Can Brazil actually deliver on what it promises abroad? Brasilia's influence depends on partners believing that today’s deals will survive tomorrow’s politics, and that this belief is eroding.More than 90 per cent of the federal government’s non-interest spending is mandatory, leaving little room for infrastructure, which Brazil needs if it is to make use of its mineral reserves.The International Monetary Fund (IMF) projects that government debt will reach about 98 per cent of GDP by the end of 2026. Real interest rates sit near 10 per cent, so servicing that debt consumes funds that could strengthen security forces or support strategic goals.Adding to that, criminal networks operate across more than 1,500 clandestine airstrips in the Amazon basin and move drugs, gold and weapons across borders with Brazil’s ten neighbours.Responsibility for fighting them is split among federal police, highway police, an intelligence agency, police forces in 26 states and the federal district, the armed forces and prosecutors. Efforts to bring them under one authority have failed in Congress. The result is that decisions about gangs operating from Brazilian soil are increasingly taken elsewhere, as Washington’s terrorist designations show.The third problem is trust in the courts because since late 2025, the public has learned how far parts of the judiciary became entangled with the Banco Master affair.The bank’s owner is alleged to have made side payments and awarded lucrative contracts to families of Supreme Court justices, and to have lent his private jets to justices.Flavio Bolsonaro is himself under investigation over alleged links to the bank, and figures close to Lula’s government have also been drawn in.The winner will appoint at least three of the court’s 11 justices, reshaping the institution that is meant to hold the next government to account.The neighbourhood also offers little relief. Brazil once led the creation of regional institutions such as Mercosur, but it is now increasingly isolated in South America. Its relationship with Argentina, which helped underpin four decades of regional stability, has deteriorated to the point that neither country has an ambassador in the other’s capital.Where India standsIndia could probably be the member with the most to lose from a Brics that becomes either a Chinese-led counterweight to the West or an empty shell.India has a significant interest in Brazil's political direction, given its economic ties with the Latin American nation. Bilateral trade exceeded $15 billion in 2025, making Brazil India's biggest trading partner in Latin America. Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva have set a target of taking bilateral trade to $20 billion by 2030.Brazil's importance also extends to the steel sector, as the country is a major global supplier of iron ore and has substantial reserves of minerals used in steel production. Stronger cooperation could help India secure vital raw materials and access technologies needed to support the long-term expansion of its steel industry, according to a government statement.Flavio Bolsonaro, meanwhile, has indicated that he would not align himself exclusively with any side, naming India among the countries with which he would maintain engagement.India and Brazil have shared a strategic partnership since 2006, with collaboration covering areas such as defence, energy, agriculture, healthcare, critical minerals, technology and digital infrastructure.Beyond trade, the two countries coordinate on several international issues, including reform of the United Nations, climate change and counter-terrorism. Brazil is also India's largest trading partner across Latin America and the Caribbean.India hosted this year’s summit, where the Iranian and Emirati presidents both turned up, and it shares Brazil’s view that the bloc should push for reform rather than confrontation.ALSO READ | Bombs without brakes? Why the US-China AI race may be harder to control than the nuclear oneThe two countries also sit together in Partners for Multilateralism, launched on 21 September alongside Canada, Australia, Barbados, the European Union and Kenya.The framework is meant to support international law and institutional reform, and it links western and Global South middle powers without forcing any of them to pick a camp.That makes Lula a natural partner for New Delhi, and a Bolsonaro victory a quiet setback that could probably interrupt the bloc's ambitions.India would lose a like-minded voice for a measured, rules-based Brics, leaving it with partners who are either more radical or more distant. Its own position, balancing Washington and Beijing, depends on a bloc that can talk to both.However, whichever way Brazil votes, nobody expects an immediate revolution in its foreign policy.Rubens Ricupero, a former Brazilian diplomat, calls Bolsonaro’s approach a “blank slate”, while Lula’s is well established. The market for Brazil’s minerals, the weight of its trade with China and the limits on its finances will constrain either man. The pressure will come from outside.Rubens Barbosa, a former Brazilian ambassador to the US, warns that “the Americans may prove reluctant to yield anything to Lula, preferring to wait and negotiate with Bolsonaro.”Economist Monica de Bolle argues that a re-elected Lula facing a right-leaning Congress would feel “a lot of pressure” to give in “to some US demands regarding natural resources, as well as other issues.”That is the real stake for Brics on 25 October. The bloc’s future will turn on whether Brazil stays a champion of its reformist wing or becomes a member that merely turns up.ALSO READ | UN-doing the United Nations: Can its next chief fix a system under severe strain?You use AI every day. articles.title: Pakistan ranks lowest in South Asia on hunger index amid rising food prices
articles.summary: Pakistan has recorded the poorest performance in South Asia in the 2026 global hunger index (GHI), reflecting mounting food insecurity driven by economic
articles.body: Pakistan has recorded the poorest performance in South Asia in the 2026 global hunger index (GHI), reflecting mounting food insecurity driven by economic instability, rising food prices, climate-related disasters and international conflicts, according to a report by Dawn.Titled “No Security Without Food Security”, the report was jointly prepared by German aid organisation Welthungerhilfe, the institute for international law of peace and armed conflict at Ruhr university Bochum, and swiss organisation helvetas.According to the news agency ANI, the findings indicate that progress in reducing hunger across South Asia has largely stagnated, while Pakistan and Afghanistan have experienced a deterioration in conditions since 2018.Economic crisis and food inflation worsen Pakistan’s hunger situationPakistan’s economic challenges and persistent food inflation have eroded household purchasing power, making it increasingly difficult for families to access sufficient and nutritious food.The report noted that Pakistan’s undernourishment indicator had deteriorated from a low level in 2018 to a medium level. Meanwhile, child wasting has approached the threshold associated with the high category, underscoring continuing concerns over child nutrition.Hunger reduction stalls across South AsiaSouth Asia recorded an overall global hunger index score of 23.5, placing the region in the serious category. While the score represents an improvement from 37.5 in 2000, the report suggests that much of the progress was achieved before 2018.Over the past two decades, Pakistan and Afghanistan have moved out of the alarming hunger category. However, persistent levels of child malnutrition continue to pose a significant challenge in both countries.Child stunting has continued to decline in Pakistan, while Afghanistan has recorded a slight increase in the indicator since 2018.Child mortality rates have improved in both countries, falling from very high levels in 2000 to medium levels in the latest assessment.Extreme weather threatens regional food productionThe report also drew attention to the growing impact of extreme weather events on agricultural production and food security across South Asia.Heavy rainfall and flooding damaged crops in parts of Pakistan and Bangladesh. In Afghanistan, inadequate rainfall and unusually high temperatures disrupted the cereal-growing season in 2026.These climate-related pressures could further aggravate food shortages and prolong acute food insecurity across the region, according to Dawn.Millions across South Asia continue to face undernourishmentEstimates from the food and agriculture organisation (FAO) indicate that approximately 218 million people across South Asia, including Iran, experienced undernourishment between 2023 and 2025.This represents roughly one-third of the global population affected by undernourishment during the period, highlighting the scale of the region’s food security challenge.The findings underscore the need for sustained efforts to address economic vulnerabilities, improve access to nutritious food and strengthen agricultural resilience against climate-related shocks.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Not wanted': Irish hotel reportedly cancels 70 rooms reserved for antisemitism conference attendees
articles.summary: Jewish Representative Council of Ireland chairman Maurice Cohen says a Dublin hotel rejected an antisemitism conference after its manager questioned IDF involvement.
articles.body: A Dublin hotel declined to host an international event focused on combating antisemitism and subsequently withdrew approximately 70 rooms reserved for delegates after its general manager questioned whether the Israel Defense Forces would be involved, according to a Jewish community leader who attended the meeting. Maurice Cohen, chairman of the Jewish Representative Council of Ireland, told Fox News Digital that he and an event organizer met with representatives of the Herbert Park Hotel, including its general manager, on May 7 to explain the gathering and discuss arrangements. The event was connected to this week's Special Envoys and Coordinators Combating Antisemitism Conference, which brought Jewish leaders, diplomats and government officials responsible for confronting antisemitism to Dublin, Ireland. IRISH PM REJECTS ANTISEMITISM CONCERNS IN IRELAND AMID DRAMATIC VOTE OVER BOYCOTTING ISRAEL GAME Cohen said organizers had received written confirmation that approximately 70 rooms were being held for participants. During the meeting, Cohen explained that the event would bring together Jewish community representatives, diplomats and government officials, many of whom were not Jewish. He said the manager’s demeanor appeared to change before she asked whether the IDF would be involved. "I was completely taken aback by that question," Cohen told Fox News Digital. "I said, ‘What would the IDF have to do with a conference on antisemitism?’" Cohen said the hotel did not answer. The general manager told him she would need to consult the hotel’s owners before deciding whether the event could proceed. On May 8, one day after the meeting, organizers received an email stating that the hotel could not accommodate their "event," Cohen said. Two to three days after the May 7 meeting, organizers followed up by asking whether the approximately 70 rooms reserved for delegates remained available. The hotel then informed them that the rooms were no longer available and claimed they had automatically been released one week before the meeting, according to Cohen. He said the hotel never mentioned that during the discussion with management. ANTISEMITIC VIOLENCE ESCALATES AS DEADLY WEAPON ATTACKS SURGE IN 2025: REPORT "Why would you hold a meeting seven days after the rooms had been canceled without mentioning them?" Cohen said. "To my mind, that excuse was a retrospective excuse." Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations, Danny Danon, told Fox News Digital, "If the reports from Dublin are accurate, this is a disgraceful example of the very antisemitism the conference was organized to combat." "Seventy rooms had been booked. Seventy people had been welcomed as guests," Cohen said during an Oct. 13 address at Ireland’s Department of Foreign Affairs. "The only thing that changed was what they were understood to be." The experience was personal for Cohen, who said he had attended meetings, New Year’s Eve celebrations and his mother’s birthdays at the hotel through her 93rd birthday. "How quickly does the word ‘Jewish’ change a conversation?" Cohen asked during his address. The disputed hotel cancellation is the latest episode to raise concerns among Jewish leaders about antisemitic discrimination in Ireland. The country has no official state mechanism dedicated to tracking antisemitic incidents, leaving community organizations to document cases and prompting concerns that many experiences are never formally recorded. FROM LONDON SYNAGOGUES TO NEW YORK PRESCHOOLS — ANTISEMITIC ATTACKS ESCALATING ON BOTH SIDES OF THE ATLANTIC Ireland’s Jewish community numbers only about 2,200 people. Against that backdrop, the Jewish Representative Council of Ireland recorded 143 self-reported antisemitic incidents through its first six-month reporting initiative, including verbal abuse, threats, vandalism and discrimination. The council cautioned that the findings represent only a partial picture because antisemitism is often underreported. Cohen said the atmosphere for Ireland’s small Jewish community has deteriorated since the Oct. 7 Hamas terrorist attacks, describing the wider climate facing Jewish and Israeli people in Ireland as "ambient antisemitism." Fox News Digital sent questions to the Irish government asking whether it condemns the hotel’s reported actions and whether any review or investigation is being considered. The office of Prime Minister Micheál Martin, the government departments responsible for foreign affairs and justice, and the Irish Embassy in Washington, D.C., were contacted for comment. None had responded at the time of publication. In an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital in September, Martin said, "We have no toleration for antisemitism, none." SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER "It’s all around us," Cohen told Fox News Digital. "If you say you’re Israeli, you may not get into certain places. The narrative is so one-sided." When Fox News Digital reached the Herbert Park Hotel directly by phone and asked about Cohen’s account, the decision to reject the event and the subsequent release of approximately 70 rooms, a hotel representative responded, "No comment." Cohen said the hotel’s management should speak directly with Jewish community representatives and receive training on contemporary antisemitism. "They need training on what antisemitism is," Cohen told Fox News Digital. "They need to be cognizant of the fact they are promoting antisemitism. They need to understand why they’re so wrong." Cohen said several Irish lawmakers and civil servants contacted him personally after his Oct. 13 address, though he had not seen a broader public condemnation from the Irish government. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I, like most people, don’t want to be in a place where I’m not wanted," Cohen said. Fox News Digital also reached out to the owners of the hotel through its corporate entity but did not receive a response by the time of publication.

articles.title: ‘Please pretend I’m running’: Trump urges voters to back Republicans in US midterm elections
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has urged voters to treat the November 3 midterm elections as a referendum on his presidency, warning that Democrats could undo
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has urged voters to treat the November 3 midterm elections as a referendum on his presidency, warning that Democrats could undo his administration’s policies if they regain control of Congress.Trump, who is not eligible to run in the congressional elections as a candidate, made the appeal while campaigning for Republican candidates in Arizona and preparing to travel to Montana. He said he planned to hold around 32 or 33 rallies before election day to boost Republican turnout.“So essentially I’m saying, ‘Please pretend I’m running.’ And in a true sense, I am running because I don’t want them tearing down what we’ve built,” Trump told reporters.The President said he had already held about eight rallies and claimed Republican voter turnout fell by 49 per cent when he was not personally on the ballot, without providing evidence for the figure.“When I don’t run, which, you know, in theory I’m not running, but I feel that I’m running. When I don’t run, we get 49 per cent less turnout,” he said.Trump repeated the message at a rally in Bullhead City, Arizona, where he campaigned for Republican gubernatorial candidate Andy Biggs.“So I’m here to say, please pretend I’m on the ballot,” he told supporters.The President has framed the midterm elections as a crucial test of his second-term agenda, urging Republicans to retain control of both chambers of Congress. He warned that a Democratic victory could put his administration’s tax policies, border enforcement measures and other priorities at risk.Trump promises $5,000 payments if Republicans winDuring his campaign push, Trump also promised a potential $5,000 payment to adult American citizens if Republicans retain control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate.He said the proposed payments would be funded through tariff revenue and economic growth, adding that the money would have to be spent within the United States. However, he did not outline how the proposal would be authorised or implemented.Trump’s campaign schedule includes visits to Republican strongholds as well as states where competitive congressional races could influence the balance of power in Washington. He named Ohio and Texas among the states he planned to visit, besides Montana and Michigan.Asked why he was travelling to Montana, a state he described as strongly supportive of him, Trump said he wanted to ensure Republicans won.“Montana, because we wanna make sure we win,” he said.The November 3 elections will determine control of the House of Representatives and a portion of the Senate. While Trump is not on the ballot, the results will determine how easily his administration can pass legislation and could lead to greater congressional scrutiny if Democrats take control of either chamber.The party holding the White House has often faced setbacks in midterm elections. Losing either chamber could complicate Trump’s legislative agenda and strengthen Democratic oversight during the final two years of his current term.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: '4 Russian Su-34s destroyed, 2 more hit': Zelenskyy makes big claim, shares photo
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Thursday claimed that Ukraine had destroyed four Russian Su-34 fighter-bombers and damaged two others in an
articles.body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Thursday claimed that Ukraine had destroyed four Russian Su-34 fighter-bombers and damaged two others in an overnight strike on the Borisoglebsk airfield in Russia’s Voronezh region. Ukraine’s military said it had confirmed damage to all six aircraft, while Zelenskyy said the attack was carried out using a Neptune missile.In a post on X, Zelenskyy said the aircraft were loaded with aerial bombs and ready to launch fresh attacks on Ukraine. He shared a photo alongside his statement."The Russians used them to terrorize our people. These very warplanes were ready to launch new attacks on Ukraine and were loaded with aerial bombs," Zelenskyy said."Our Long Neptune missile was used to strike the target. I thank the warriors of the Ukrainian Navy for their precision!"Ukraine’s military general staff said on Telegram that it had confirmed varying degrees of damage to all six Su-34 aircraft in the overnight operation.The Su-34M is a fighter-bomber frequently used by Russian forces to drop glide bombs on Ukrainian cities near the frontline. Each aircraft costs tens of millions of US dollars.Ukraine claims further strikes on Russian targetsZelenskyy also said Ukraine had struck a facility in Russia’s Oryol region used to store and launch attack drones. He added that another target had been hit in the Black Sea."Our long-range sanctions also reached a site in the Oryol region used to store and launch attack drones. A target was also hit in the Black Sea," he said.Describing the operations as a response to Russian attacks, Zelenskyy said Ukraine would continue its long-range strikes as Moscow was prolonging the war."These are our justified responses to all of Russia’s terror against Ukraine. Russia is dragging out the war, so our long-range operations will continue."

articles.title: Flynn urges prime minister to 'bring it on' over independence referendum
articles.summary: The SNP's Stephen Flynn tells his party's conference independence supporters are "winning the argument".
articles.body:
SNP minister Stephen Flynn has called on the prime minister to "bring it on" and let the people of Scotland decide the country's future in an independence referendum.

Flynn, the party's former Westminster leader and now transport secretary at Holyrood, said the independence movement was facing its greatest-ever challenge.

But he insisted "we are winning the argument" and told delegates at the SNP conference in Aberdeen that "all of us should feel pride in how far our movement has come".

It comes after Prime Minister Andy Burnham told MPs a border poll would be considered in both Scotland and Northern Ireland if there was a clear consensus and public opinion had changed.

The PM later moved to clarify his position by telling First Minister John Swinney a second Scottish independence referendum remains "off limits".

Flynn told SNP members on the opening day of the conference that the party's focus was firmly on independence, with a major new campaign being announced.

He said: "Look at where we stand now – three nations of the UK whose leaders are committed to constitutional change, a British prime minister telling us we can have our independence when the people of Scotland want it.

"All of us should feel pride in how far our movement has come."

He added: "We are winning the argument, we can see that by reading the newspapers or listening to the panic of unionist politicians."

But Flynn warned there was "no shortcut" to achieving independence.

"One by one, we must persuade our families, our friends, our neighbours, of our cause. One by one, step by step," he said.

"It takes effort, it takes patient persuasion, it takes hard graft, but we can see that it is working and it is precisely because it is working that the period ahead will be the greatest challenge our movement has ever faced.

"With the weight of Scottish public opinion moving to our cause, we will see that final lap through together – for Scotland."

Swinney will bring the SNP's three-day conference to a close with a keynote speech to delegates on Saturday.

He is expected to promote his renewed push for independence, having said he wants to hold a second independence referendum by 2031.

The Supreme Court has ruled that the Scottish government is unable to do so without the consent of Westminster.

articles.title: In 2014, Chip and Joanna Gaines bought a 2.6-acre former cottonseed mill in Waco; 12 years later, the Magnolia site spans about 5.3 acres with shops, a bakery, coffee shop, ball field and restored 1894 church
articles.summary: Two huge, 120-foot-tall, rust-coloured grain silos dominate the skyline of central Waco, Texas.
articles.body: Two huge, 120-foot-tall, rust-coloured grain silos dominate the skyline of central Waco, Texas. They serve as a landmark for millions of visitors every year. In 2014, television personalities Chip and Joanna Gaines bought a 2.6-acre former cottonseed mill on the site. Twelve years later, their flagship Magnolia property has grown to about 5.3 acres. It now covers almost an entire city block and includes retail shops, a bakery, a coffee shop, a Wiffle ball field, and a restored 19th-century church. What started as one retail building alongside two unused industrial structures has grown into a major tourist destination for the city.Expanding the downtown footprintWhen Chip and Joanna Gaines first bought the property in 2014, its main attraction was a 12,000-square-foot former grain barn. It became the original Magnolia Market retail store. The couple wanted to turn the neglected industrial site into a shared space where families could gather. According to official planning details published on the company's website, Magnolia began a major expansion of the grounds in 2020. The project doubled the site from its original 2.6 acres to about 5.3 acres. The company added nearby lots to make room for more shops, dining options, and green spaces. The expansion turned the property from a simple home decor store into a larger, walkable campus where visitors can explore different attractions.Restoring a piece of Waco historyOne of the main additions to the expanded grounds is the Old Church, a historic wooden building originally built in 1894. According to historical notes released by Magnolia, the church had fallen into poor condition at its original location elsewhere in Waco before it was moved to the Silos property. Workers moved the entire wooden church to the corner of 8th Street. They spent several years restoring it while preserving its original stained-glass windows, heart pine flooring, and exposed wooden frame. The restored building now stands near the main public entrance as a quiet reminder of local history. Visitors can sit inside and look out over the surrounding grounds. Six special boutique shops line the walkways leading to the Old Church. Designed as small, separate cottages, the shops sell a range of carefully chosen products. These include men's clothing, paper goods, retro-style indoor plants, and handmade jewellery.Rebuilding a legendary ballparkBeyond the shops, the expanded grounds also celebrate local sports history with the addition of Katy Ballpark. Historical property records cited in Magnolia's archive show that the land directly behind the original cottonseed mill was once home to Katy Park, a well-known local baseball stadium that opened in 1905. Over the years, famous professional baseball players, including Babe Ruth and Lou Gehrig, played exhibition games there. To honour that history, Chip and Joanna Gaines built a smaller Wiffle ball field on the exact site of the historic ballpark. Katy Ballpark has artificial turf, a traditional wooden outfield fence, a scoreboard, and a concession stand. The stand sells takeaway food, soft pretzels, and ice cream. "Our vision for the Silos has always been to offer a place where people could gather and spend time together," Joanna Gaines wrote in a statement on the company blog when the expansion was announced. "It's really an honour every time someone chooses to walk through those gates, and it's important to Chip and me that the experiences we create across the grounds are unique and meaningful, and offer something for everyone."Dining options and public spacesAlong with the ballpark and retail cottages, the property has several different places to eat and drink. Magnolia Press is a full-service coffee shop inside a restored brick warehouse. It has an outdoor courtyard with a wood-burning fireplace and seating. Nearby, Silos Baking Co. operates from a converted historic building along the edge of the property. It makes baked goods for thousands of visitors each day. The central lawn includes a dedicated area for local food trucks, with shaded wooden picnic tables where visitors can eat outdoors. The two 120-foot-tall steel-and-concrete grain silos remain empty and closed to the public for safety reasons. Even so, they continue to serve as the property's main architectural landmark. Twelve years after the original purchase, the expanded 5.3-acre site remains a major centre for tourism and economic activity in downtown Waco.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Trump calls off livestream of Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad
articles.summary: Trump said some would "rather not watch" the killing of Nidal Hasan, the first military execution in over 60 years.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has called off plans to livestream the execution of former US army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan by firing squad.

Trump had previously said he approved of showing the death of the Fort Hood attacker, while Vice-President JD Vance cast doubt on whether it would happen and said he would not watch it.

Trump's decision to cancel the livestream came after widespread criticism in the US and globally. On Thursday, he said that "many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die".

"I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan," Trump said.

"He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," the president added.

Hasan fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at a military base in Texas in 2009, injuring another 32. His execution by firing squad will be the first military execution in more than 60 years.

Trump said the families of the victims can still view the execution in person if they wish.

"They deserve to witness JUSTICE!" he said.

After the Pentagon announced last week that it would execute Hasan on 3 December 2026 by firing squad and livestream the event, a cascade of criticism quickly followed from human rights groups and many others. The United Nations called the plans "abhorrent".

While there were more than 2,700 executions across 17 countries last year, only two nations carried them out publicly. According to Amnesty International, 11 public executions were known to have been carried out in Iran in 2025 and another six in Afghanistan.

US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth defended his decision to air Hasan's execution online, saying that "people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things".

But as criticism mounted, Trump appeared to hedge his support, saying on Friday that he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan, but adding that the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it.

The president also called Hasan "totally nuts".

"I really don't care how he goes, as long as he goes, and I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him," he said.

John Galligan, a lawyer for Hasan working primarily on civil issues, told the BBC that Trump's decision to cancel the livestream of his execution "comes as no surprise".

"It was initially a dumb decision and statement by Hegseth to livestream any execution - and it violated the Army's own regulation," Galligan said.

He said Hasan is paralysed from the chest down, something that Trump "allegedly didn't even know" when he approved the livestream plan.

"The damage has already been done - the Army is now just trying to clean up the mess," Galligan said. "It will permanently remain a stain on our military justice system."

He added that it was not clear if Hasan was aware yet of Trump's "reversal" of the livestream decision.

Hasan opened fire in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines.

He later admitted in court that he was the gunman and apologised for "any mistakes". He said during his court-martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military.

The killings on 5 November 2009 were the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base.

US military law requires that a military execution be approved by the US president. It also requires appellate review, when a higher court inspects the decision and gives a final judgement on its legality to move forward.

articles.title: Supreme Court seeks Centre’s response on plea to hold protest organisers liable for damage
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Thursday sought responses from the Centre, Delhi Police and others on a plea seeking to hold organisers of protests
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Thursday sought responses from the Centre, Delhi Police and others on a plea seeking to hold organisers of protests personally or jointly liable for loss of life, injuries, damage to public or private property and the costs incurred by the authorities.A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi was hearing the petition, which also sought a direction that protests, dharnas, demonstrations, processions and public assemblies in the national capital should not be held without prior written permission from the competent authority.The plea sought to make organisers, callers, leaders or convenors of protests liable for losses arising from unlawful acts or omissions, including when an assembly is held without permission or violates the conditions imposed for its approval.The bench issued notices to the Centre, Delhi Police and other parties, seeking their responses to the petition, according to news agency PTI.Plea seeks designated protest sites in DelhiThe petition also sought directions to the authorities to identify and notify designated locations for protests, dharnas, demonstrations and public assemblies in Delhi. These sites, it said, should be situated away from densely populated, commercial and central areas.It further proposed that every application seeking permission for a protest, demonstration, procession or public assembly should be accompanied by an affidavit from the organiser disclosing the source of funding.The declaration should also specify whether any part of the funds had been received, or was expected to be received, from a foreign source or an unidentified source, the plea said.According to the petition, a false or incomplete declaration should provide grounds for revoking permission, recovering compensation and costs from the organiser and those found to have financed the assembly, and initiating prosecution in accordance with the law.Supreme Court hears multiple pleas linked to Delhi protestsThe hearing came as the Supreme Court considered several petitions connected to protests in Delhi, including pleas concerning alleged assaults on journalists and lawyers, police action and restrictions on demonstrations.In a separate matter, the bench issued notices to the Centre and the Delhi government on a plea challenging the Delhi Police’s decision to de-notify Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site.The petitioner, advocate Swaty Malik, argued that removing the designation violated the fundamental right to protest. The plea maintained that demonstrations should be permitted at a location where protesters could make their grievances heard by the state administration.Justice Bagchi observed that the concept of being heard should also be considered in the context of technology.“The word ‘heard’ must be used in the perspective of technology also”, Justice Bagchi remarked.The court agreed to examine the petition and sought responses from the authorities.In other pleas linked to the protests, the Supreme Court sought responses from the authorities over allegations involving journalists and lawyers. It also directed law-enforcement agencies to preserve CCTV footage and other digital records relating to the demonstrations.The bench further directed that the order issued under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) be placed on record. The provision empowers authorised executive magistrates to issue urgent prohibitory orders to prevent public danger, disturbances or riots.The court indicated that the Union government would file a consolidated response to the batch of petitions while relevant material relating to individual cases was preserved.Court also takes up pleas on voter roll revisionSeparately, the Supreme Court issued notices to the Election Commission and chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar on a petition filed by Congress leader Rahul Gandhi and 12 other opposition leaders over alleged large-scale voter deletions and irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The bench also took note of submissions concerning the October 12 march to the Supreme Court by Rahul and other opposition leaders.“Nobody can browbeat us (judiciary),” CJI Surya Kant said during the hearing, adding that the court was aware of statements made both inside and outside the courtroom.The court said it would ask one of the petitioners about his conduct at the next hearing, without naming the individual.The petition by Rahul and the other opposition leaders sought an independent audit of deletions and modifications made during the SIR, to be conducted by a committee headed by a retired Supreme Court judge and assisted by technical experts and other prominent citizens.It also sought safeguards against deleting voters’ names without notice and a reasonable opportunity to be heard, along with measures to allow eligible voters in Punjab and other poll-bound states to seek inclusion in electoral rolls within the time permitted by law.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Gardaí (Irish police) have arrested a man aged in his 20s and a woman in her 30s in connection with a suspected arson attack which killed four family members in Waterford.

They are currently being held in a station in the east of the Republic of Ireland.

Kim English, Philip English and two of their children - nine-year-old Jayden and 12-year-old Callum - died after their home in Birch Avenue, on the outskirts of Waterford was set on fire on Tuesday.

Two other children who were also in the house at the time remain in a critical condition in hospital in Crumlin in Dublin.

Post mortems on the four deceased family members have been carried out but their results are not being released for "operational reasons".

Officers have also appealed for anybody with information on the "murderous attack" to come forward and have also appealed for dash cam footage.

articles.title: Hole in Neanderthal shoulder bone linked to ancient wooden spear
articles.summary: A 75,000-year-old Neanderthal spear wound may be evidence violence shaped human life far earlier than thought.
articles.body:
A Neanderthal who died 75,000 years ago may have been struck through the chest by a sharpened wooden spear, archaeologists say.

They say a 15mm hole found in a shoulder blade in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan could be the earliest evidence of lethal violence involving such a weapon.

From the angle of the wound and other evidence, the researchers believe the spear entered the individual's chest and passed through the body - probably damaging a lung and major blood vessels - and exited through the left shoulder blade to leave a near-perfect hole.

The research is the latest in emerging evidence that suggests Neanderthal societies experienced more violence than previously thought.

Neanderthals were a separate species of humans that went extinct around 40,000 years ago. They lived across a large expanse of Europe and western and central Asia, and sometimes overlapped with our species, Homo sapiens.

The wounded Neanderthal's remains were found in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan. As well as the left shoulder blade, the individual's right hand, three ribs and some teeth were also found.

A hole in the shoulder blade may be the earliest evidence of "lethal interpersonal violence" from a wooden spear, according to Dr Emma Pomeroy, study lead author from Cambridge's Department of Archaeology.

"The fatal strike may have been an intended heart shot," she told BBC News.

Archaeologists call the remains Shanidar A, named after the cave in which they were found. Remains of at least 10 Neanderthals were discovered in excavations in the cave in the 1950s.

The wound is thought to be the first evidence for use of sharpened wooden spears in the prehistoric Middle East, according to Pomeroy.

"It is not the kind of break that you would get naturally, because it is so circular," she said. "Experiments with reconstructed wooden spears produce very similar round holes in bone."

But the interpersonal violence is by no means certain, she says. It may be a case of friendly fire, a wound caused as a result of a hunting accident.

But Prof Chris Stringer of the Natural History Museum in London, who was not involved in the research, told BBC News that an attack by a rival was the more plausible explanation.

"The researchers leave it open whether this resulted from a hunting accident or interpersonal violence, but in my view the latter seems more likely, given the positioning and extent of the wound," he said.

This discovery has echoes of an earlier find in the same cave, in 1957. Those remains involved another Neanderthal who lived more recently, around 50, 000 years ago. Their ribs had evidence of a partly healed wound, which archaeologists believe was probably caused by a stone-tipped spear.

We can't tell for sure whether these Neanderthals were hurt by a companion during a hunt or murdered by a rival. But they join a small but growing body of evidence which point to the possibility that human-on-human violence was more common and goes back further than the current scientific consensus would suggest.

"I unfortunately see the growing body of evidence as an indication that interpersonal violence goes deep into human prehistory," Stringer told BBC News.

A key piece of that evidence is a study published in 2022 of very early Neanderthal skulls from northern Spain at an archaeological site called "the Pit of Bones". It suggests that deadly violence was taking place about 430,000 years ago.

Researchers found 57 healed head injuries among 20 individuals. Nine individuals had potentially fatal skull fractures. Six had similar puncture wounds at the back-left of the head. Because the wounds repeatedly occurred in almost the same place, the researchers concluded that deliberate blows were more likely than accidental damage. One skull had two wounds that had probably been inflicted with the same object.

The Pit of Bones findings do not show that everyone in this population was habitually violent, but they provide strong evidence that repeated killing occurred among these people hundreds of thousands of years ago.

For decades, many archaeologists linked the beginnings of organised warfare to farming, when people began living in permanent settlements and competing over land, livestock and food stores.

But evidence from earlier hunter-gatherers and still older human relatives has since shown that individual killings pre-date farming by a very long way.

The live scientific debate is over how common such violence was, and when sporadic attacks became organised conflict and wars between groups.

The research has been published in the journal Scientific Reports.

articles.title: Andhra SEC appoints 28 IAS officers as poll observers
articles.summary: Andhra Pradesh SEC appoints 28 IAS officers as general observers for local body polls, directing strict model code compliance, security coordination and fair voting.
articles.body: Vijayawada: The State Election Commission (SEC) has appointed 28 IAS officers as general observers to oversee the conduct of local body elections in Andhra Pradesh, directing them to ensure free, fair, transparent and impartial polling across the state.State election commissioner Anil Chandra Punetha, who briefed the officers on Thursday, said the model code of conduct had come into force with the announcement of the election schedule and instructed the observers to closely monitor violations and ensure strict compliance with election rules.Punetha emphasised that every voter should be able to exercise their franchise without fear, pressure or inducement. He asked the observers to guide officials at all levels and ensure that the election process remained peaceful and impartial.The general observers have been tasked with monitoring the implementation of election rules and ensuring transparency at every stage of the poll process. They were also instructed to coordinate with district police authorities to ensure adequate security arrangements and prevent any untoward incidents during the elections.Highlighting the role of technology in election management, Punetha drew the officers’ attention to the Poll Management App developed by SEC. The application provides information relating to voter management, polling stations and election procedures, helping officials monitor and manage the process more effectively.The commissioner stressed that observers should remain vigilant throughout the election process and take appropriate steps to address violations of the model code of conduct. Their role would be crucial in ensuring that election officials discharge their duties impartially and that political parties and candidates adhere to the prescribed rules.SEC’s deployment of IAS officers as general observers is aimed at strengthening supervision and accountability during the local body elections, with particular emphasis on maintaining a level playing field for contestants and protecting voters’ rights.Punetha called upon the observers to uphold the principles of fairness and transparency and ensure that the elections were conducted in a manner that inspires public confidence in the democratic process.Senior IAS officers S Nagalakshmi, M Seshagiribabu, KVN Chakradhar Babu, K Kannababu, MM Nayak, Ch Sridhar, Manjeer Jilani, Hebsiba Rani, Ranjit Basha, Sivasankar Lotheti, Shanmohan, M Gouthami, P Arun Babu, P Prasanthi, Lavanya Veni, Bhargavi, JV Murali, TS Chetan, Kurmanath, R Gopalakrishna, Praveen Aditya, Tej Bharath, Geethanjali Sharma were appointed as general observers. articles.title: Maduro pleads not guilty to additional charges in New York
articles.summary: "I reject this document entirely," Maduro said in court, responding to newly added torture-related charges.
articles.body:
Venezuela's former leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, appeared in court on Thursday to plead not guilty to new charges of conspiracy to commit torture.

The US government initially accused Maduro of narco-terrorism, drug trafficking and weapons-related offenses, before adding new charges against him and Flores last week.

Maduro and Flores were captured in January during a US military raid, after which they were taken to New York, where they remain in jail.

The couple has pleaded not guilty to the allegations and both have argued to have the case thrown out on the grounds that they qualify for sovereign immunity. Their trial is scheduled for June 2027.

In a new indictment last week, government prosecutors alleged Maduro and Flores "created and maintained a violent system of repression" that saw "thousands of Venezuelans" killed, harassed, and tortured.

Nicolas Maduro denied the new charges brought against him by the US government, telling a court on Thursday he denied the "false accusations and false testimony behind him."

"I reject this document entirely," Maduro said in Spanish through a translator.

Judge Alvin Hellerstein interrupted Maduro, and declared the court would enter a plea of not guilty for Maduro.

"I am completely innocent. I am not guilty," Flores said through a translator.

Maduro and Flores wore beige jail uniforms and both appear to have lost weight during their detention in Brooklyn.

The alleged torture methods included "electric shock, asphyxiation, rape, forced nudity, prolonged isolation, starvation, punishment cells, and psychological torture", the indictment states.

The US also accused Maduro of authorising the use of torture "against specific individuals" and alleges US citizens were tortured under this system.

Prosecutors already have accused Maduro, his wife and son, and their accomplices of engaging in a cocaine-trafficking conspiracy and partnering with cartels designated as terrorist groups.

Maduro previously called such charges a tool to further "imperial" plans for getting access to Venezuela's rich oil reserves.

He and his wife's lawyers have argued that Maduro is the leader of a sovereign country and therefore immune from prosecution. They contend the US taking him by force is illegal.

Flores unsuccessfully petitioned a judge to allow her to be released on bond while she awaited trial, arguing she had heart problems and other health issues while detained at the notorious Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn.
